title: Job 13:17–28
context: Job continues, still speaking to his friends at first and then directly to God. He announces that he has prepared his case and knows he is righteous, meaning innocent of the charges that would explain his suffering. He asks God to remove his hand and terror, then to call or answer him, and to show him his sins. He ends with a complaint that God hides his face and treats him as an enemy. Job's words are bold. The book does not condemn Job for seeking God, but the LORD will later answer him out of the whirlwind (38:1).

verses.text: Listen carefully to my speech. Let my declaration be in your ears.
verses.arminianNotes: "Listen carefully to my speech." Arminian readers see Job asking the friends to hear his declaration as a formal statement in a court case.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the call to listen sets up Job's claim of innocence in the next verse. He wants his words heard fully before any judgment is made.

verses.text: See now, I have set my cause in order. I know that I am righteous.
verses.arminianNotes: "See now, I have set my cause in order. I know that I am righteous." Arminian readers read "righteous" as innocent of the specific wrongs the friends imply, not as a claim to sinless perfection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read Job's claim as legal innocence in this case. He admits "the iniquities of my youth" in verse 26, so he is not claiming never to have sinned.

verses.text: Who is he who will contend with me? For then I would hold my peace and give up the spirit.
verses.arminianNotes: "Who is he who will contend with me?" Arminian readers see Job's confidence that no one can prove him guilty, and his willingness to die if someone could.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job says that if anyone could prove him wrong, he would "hold my peace and give up the spirit." His certainty is strong, though he still lacks a hearing.

verses.text: “Only don’t do two things to me, then I will not hide myself from your face:
verses.arminianNotes: "Only don’t do two things to me." Arminian readers see Job now turning to address God directly, asking for two conditions so that he can come before God without hiding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the shift from speaking to the friends to speaking to God. Job wants to face God, but only if God will relieve the terror that overwhelms him.

verses.text: withdraw your hand far from me, and don’t let your terror make me afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks God to "withdraw your hand far from me." Arminian readers see the first request: that God remove the suffering that crushes him. The second is that God's "terror" not make him afraid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job feels God's hand as heavy affliction. He cannot argue his case while overwhelmed. Both traditions see an honest prayer from a suffering believer.

verses.text: Then call, and I will answer, or let me speak, and you answer me.
verses.arminianNotes: "Then call, and I will answer." Arminian readers see Job offering God either role: God may speak first, or Job may speak and God answer. He wants real dialogue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job's longing for an answer will be fulfilled, though not as he expects, when the LORD speaks out of the whirlwind (38:1). Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: How many are my iniquities and sins? Make me know my disobedience and my sin.
verses.arminianNotes: "How many are my iniquities and sins?" Arminian readers see Job asking God to make known any wrong that explains his suffering. He is willing to be shown his sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the request, "Make me know my disobedience and my sin." Job is not hiding from correction; he wants the charges named, as in 10:2, "Show me why you contend with me."

verses.text: Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy?
verses.arminianNotes: "Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy?" Arminian readers hear Job's deepest pain: not only loss and sickness, but the sense that God has turned away from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reader knows from 2:3 that God still calls Job "my servant." Job's sense of being God's enemy is real to him but not the full truth.

verses.text: Will you harass a driven leaf? Will you pursue the dry stubble?
verses.arminianNotes: "Will you harass a driven leaf?" Arminian readers see Job's image of himself as fragile and powerless, a leaf or dry stubble, and his question why God would pursue something so weak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between God's great power, described in chapter 12, and Job's weakness. Job cannot see why such power would be aimed at someone so small.

verses.text: For you write bitter things against me, and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
verses.arminianNotes: "For you write bitter things against me." Arminian readers see Job feeling that God has drawn up charges against him and made him "inherit the iniquities of my youth."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Job's acknowledgment of youthful sins. He does not claim perfection, but he cannot see how those sins explain his present suffering.

verses.text: You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths. You set a bound to the soles of my feet,
verses.arminianNotes: "You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths." Arminian readers see Job feeling restricted and watched, as though God were a jailer tracking every step.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the images of stocks and set bounds express Job's sense of confinement. God's close attention, which could be care, feels to him like surveillance.

verses.text: though I am decaying like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says he is "decaying like a rotten thing." Arminian readers see him ending the chapter with a picture of human frailty, wasting away "like a garment that is moth-eaten."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job's speech closes on his weakness and mortality. The chapter leaves the lawsuit open, waiting for an answer that only God can give.
